query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined experimental–modeling approach, whereby high-entropy alloy (HEA) samples are characterized by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) from low temperatures (using Debye T³‐law extrapolation for cp) up to incipient melting and then integrated with CALPHAD-based Gibbs energy modeling that explicitly accounts for configurational mixing, will yield accurate and efficient determinations of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or Al0.5CoCrFeNi) presenting a single-phase solid solution with high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled DSC measurements (with a calibrated heating rate to minimize overlapping transitions), extrapolate low-temperature heat capacity using the Debye T³ law, and then combine the DSC-derived data with CALPHAD thermodynamic assessments that incorporate mixing contributions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere with heating rates optimized for resolving latent and sensible heat contributions, while maintaining uniform sample preparation to avoid secondary phase precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy stabilizes a distorted yet uniform solid solution, leading to a pronounced and reproducible jump in cp at the melting point. This facilitates the application of the lever rule and integration methods to resolve fusion parameters, and the CALPHAD models mediate the separation of configurational and vibrational contributions.
generation.mechanism: DSC data provide direct measurements of cp(T) and latent heat (revealed as sharp increases in cp near the solidus), which, when integrated, yield the enthalpy and entropy of fusion. CALPHAD modeling supplies a thermodynamic framework that, using databases of binary (and ideally ternary) interactions, predicts Gibbs energy changes over temperature. The configurational entropy of mixing in HEAs lowers the melting temperature and modifies the driving force for crystallization, effects that are captured in the integrated approach.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to predict fusion enthalpy, entropy, melting temperature, and volume change within an approximate error margin of ±10–20% compared to conventional methods, while being applicable to a broad range of multi-component alloy systems with no pronounced secondary phase segregation.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC analysis without integration with CALPHAD modeling or without explicit consideration of configurational entropy may yield less precise and less generalizable fusion property estimates in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The method’s quantitative performance may degrade for alloys with more than five principal elements or those exhibiting substantial secondary phase precipitation, especially if reliable binary/ternary thermodynamic data are sparse.
generation.uncertainty: While DSC and CALPHAD methods are individually well-established, their combined predictive accuracy in the complex multi-dimensional HEA composition space is still subject to uncertainties stemming from incomplete thermodynamic databases and overlapping phase transitions.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of HEA compositions. For each sample, perform DSC measurements from cryogenic temperatures up through melting to obtain high-resolution cp(T) curves and latent heat signatures. In parallel, conduct CALPHAD assessments using the best available binary and ternary databases, predicting melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and changes in volume on melting. Compare the DSC-derived and CALPHAD-predicted values quantitatively.
measurements: DSC heat flow curves to determine cp(T) and latent heat jump
Integration of cp(T) data to compute entropy changes
Dilatometry or high-temperature imaging to measure volume changes at melting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined experimental and modeling approach fails to determine the fusion properties of a majority (>50%) of the tested HEAs within a ±20% error margin relative to independently validated reference values, or if systematic deviations are observed that cannot be attributed to known database limitations, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The Calphad approach is used widely in the high entropy alloys and ceramics field [,,]. Senkov et al. demonstrated [] that for high entropy alloys, Calphad computations of type and number of phases agreed well with experimental results only when more than half of binary systems were fully assessed; however, even when there are enough data on binary and ternary systems, Calphad predictions of transformation temperatures, phase compositions and fractions are challenging. Compared with metals, the databases for oxides are much more limited, especially for the temperature range addressed in this study. Nevertheless, it is instructive to compare our experimental results with Calphad predictions.

The effects of cold rolling on the phase transformation kinetics of an Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy are studied by the thermal expansion method. The transformed volume fraction–temperature curves of as-cast and 20% cold rolling Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys are determined by the lever rule method using thermal expansion curves. Using the KAS method, the mean activation energy for as-cast and deformed HEAs calculated are 181 kJ/mol and 159 kJ/mol, respectively. The kinetic exponent is determined using the local Avrami exponent method based on the JMA equation. Both as-cast and deformed samples show the three stages of kinetic exponent variations, and the deformed alloy shows a much larger value compared with the as-cast alloy, indicating a much higher nucleation and growth rate. The reason for the kinetic exponent variations are thought to be related with the deformation induced strain and defects inside the sample that can generate a much higher energy that favors the nucleation and growth process.
